findings.text: In the first paragraph a newcomer learns what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves. The what and the why are covered before any jargon appears.
findings.source: Header lede: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: The next step is linked near the top. The Next steps section then gives the clone command, the prerequisites, `./setup.sh` and a first command to try, so the newcomer knows what to do.
findings.source: Header: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself" and the Next steps section

findings.text: This is Athena's home URL, but the title and heading name a different project. Someone skimming headings or a browser tab would think the page is about firstmate, not Athena.
findings.source: <title> and h1: "Athena explains how firstmate handles work"

findings.text: Almost all of the page is detailed firstmate internals, such as exit 75, places-held and pending-close records. A newcomer who came to learn about Athena has to understand from the third lede that this is a demonstration, and nothing shows how big the demonstration is or that they can skip it.
findings.source: Sections "States of a piece of work", "Counters", "Transitions" (t1–t12), "Claims and sources" (c1–c45)

findings.text: The page never shows Athena's own output, such as a traced commit, a cost record or a verdict. The newcomer has to accept the core promise on trust. The only evidence is the study, which shows Athena reading code, not making a change.
findings.source: Header lede: "It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: A first-time visitor is not an owner and has no proposals. Putting this link in the header next to the next step is confusing and makes the reader wonder whether it applies to them.
findings.source: Header: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: The page says Athena is written in Rust but does not list a Rust toolchain, and it does not say whether setup.sh installs one. A newcomer may be unsure whether they have everything they need.
findings.source: Next steps: "Before installing, have git 2.40 or later, a C linker, curl, and either Claude Code or npm"

findings.text: It does not say which repository the command acts on (presumably the current directory) or whether it commits right away. A cautious newcomer would want to know both before pressing Enter.
findings.source: Next steps: "Try it with a one-line request: athena ask "add a changelog"... press Enter to run it on your repository."

findings.text: For a reader who stays to learn about firstmate, the up-front definitions and the glossary make the dense material approachable. The page also says plainly what it cannot tell them, for example: "The cited instruction does not say what makes work in scope."
findings.source: Start here: "Words used first" list and the Glossary

findings.text: This section refers to Athena's internal repository layout, which means nothing to a newcomer and adds no value for them.
findings.source: About this page: "the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from."
